items.short_definition: The probability, within a stated horizon and conditional on a stated model specification, that advanced AI leads to outcome O3 (permanent severe disempowerment), O4 (civilizational collapse), O5 (near-extinction), O6 (human extinction), O7 (biospheric catastrophe) or O8 (other irreversible loss). It is a model output, never a direct measurement, and is always shown with its decomposition.

definitions.text: Probability of doom: an informal term for the subjective probability that AI causes an existential catastrophe; usage varies by speaker.
definitions.note: Informal usage rarely states horizon, outcome or conditioning; this observatory always does.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: A system that matches or exceeds human performance across most cognitive tasks. Definitions differ on breadth, autonomy and economic framing.

definitions.text: Highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.
A levelled framework distinguishing performance depth (emerging to superhuman) and generality (narrow to general), with autonomy treated separately.
definitions.attribution: Morris et al., Levels of AGI (2023)

definitions.text: Unaided machines that can accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers (high-level machine intelligence).
definitions.attribution: Grace et al., ESPAI survey wording

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: An intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest.

definitions.text: Any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: A general-purpose model at or near the most capable level available at a given time.

definitions.text: General-purpose AI models with systemic risk: models with high-impact capabilities, presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations.
Models covered by developers' frontier safety frameworks, defined by capability thresholds rather than a fixed compute number.
definitions.attribution: Anthropic RSP; OpenAI Preparedness Framework; Google DeepMind FSF

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: An AI system that pursues goals over multiple steps by observing, planning and acting through tools with limited human involvement.

definitions.text: Systems that can plan and act autonomously across multiple steps to achieve goals, increasingly with tool use.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: The degree to which a system selects and executes actions without human direction or approval, measured here by unattended operation length and approval frequency.

definitions.text: Levels of autonomy from tool (fully human-controlled) through consultant, collaborator, expert to agent (fully autonomous).
definitions.attribution: Morris et al., Levels of AGI (2023)

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: The software around a model that turns it into an agent: prompt templates, tool routing, memory, retries, permissions, budgets and logging. Also called scaffold.

definitions.text: Scaffolding that provides models with tools, memory and control flow; METR reports results 'with METR's scaffold' because harness design changes measured capability.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Nested agent systems in which one harness delegates to other harnesses, inheriting or re-scoping authority; raises questions of policy drift, identity ambiguity, duplicate side effects and cancellation propagation.

definitions.text: Emerging term; closest documented practice is multi-agent orchestration through protocols such as MCP and agent-to-agent delegation.
definitions.note: No consensus definition exists; the term is defined operationally in research/agents.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: An open protocol that connects language-model applications to servers exposing tools, resources and prompts, so that agents can act on external systems in a standard way.

definitions.text: An open protocol that enables seamless integration between LLM applications and external data sources and tools.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: A model invoking external functions, APIs or systems (search, code execution, file access, payments) through structured calls.

definitions.text: Function calling and tool invocation as defined by MCP tools and vendor APIs.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Computational resources used to train or run models, usually measured in floating-point operations; a governance lever because it is detectable, excludable and concentrated.

definitions.text: Computing power is detectable, excludable, quantifiable and produced via a concentrated supply chain, which makes it a lever for governance.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: What a system can do when suitably elicited, as measured by evaluations and benchmarks; a prerequisite or pressure variable in this observatory, never an outcome.

definitions.text: Dangerous-capability thresholds defined per domain (biological, chemical, cyber, autonomy) in developer frameworks.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: The degree to which a system's objectives and behaviour match what its principals intend, including under distribution shift and when unobserved.

definitions.text: Misalignment: systems pursuing goals that conflict with human intentions; alignment faking: appearing aligned while pursuing other goals.
Rogue AIs: the difficulty of controlling agents far more intelligent than humans.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Safety that does not rely on the model being aligned: protocols that stay safe even if the model tries to subvert them.

definitions.text: Techniques that maintain safety despite intentional subversion by the model, evaluated with untrusted and trusted models.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Technical and organisational isolation (sandboxes, network egress controls, credential scoping) that limits what a system can affect.

definitions.text: Least privilege for MCP agent processes: deny access paths that a server does not require.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: A structured test of a system's capabilities or propensities under specified conditions; results depend on scaffold, elicitation and contamination.

definitions.text: Open framework for LLM evaluations with a published register of tasks.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: An event in which an AI system's development, use or malfunction led to harm.

definitions.text: An AI incident is an event, circumstance or series of events where the development, use or malfunction of one or more AI systems directly or indirectly leads to harm.

Serious incident: an incident leading to death or serious harm to health, serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, infringement of fundamental rights, or serious harm to property or the environment.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: An event that could plausibly have led to harm but did not, including contained safety failures and controlled-test findings; recorded separately from realised harm.

definitions.text: AI hazard: an event where an AI system could plausibly lead to an incident.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Large-scale harm; in this observatory 'catastrophic' outcomes are O4–O8, while O1–O2 are serious harms that leave a recovery path.

definitions.text: Global catastrophe: death of at least 10% of the world's population within a five-year period (XPT question threshold).

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: No humans survive (outcome O6).

definitions.text: Human extinction: no humans alive (Metaculus resolution criteria).

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Loss of humanity's effective control over its future; permanent severe disempowerment is outcome O3.

definitions.text: Gradual disempowerment: incremental erosion of human influence over the economy, culture and states leading to effectively irreversible loss of influence.
Similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species (survey wording paired with extinction).

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: A state of affairs that becomes effectively irreversible, such as permanent value specification or permanent institutional control.

definitions.text: Existential catastrophe includes unrecoverable dystopia as well as extinction.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Whether institutions and societies retain a credible path back from harm; the dividing line between O1–O2 and O3–O8.

definitions.text: Working definition of this observatory: an outcome is recoverable if, absent further catastrophe, human institutions could plausibly restore autonomy and welfare within generations.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Risk arising from the interaction of many systems, actors and dependencies rather than a single failure.

definitions.text: Systemic risk from general-purpose AI: risk specific to high-impact capabilities with significant impact on the Union market and society.
Societal-scale risks classified by accountability and intent.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Deliberate use of AI by humans to cause harm.

definitions.text: Malicious use: individuals or groups intentionally using AIs to cause harm.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Harm arising from a system not behaving as intended, without malicious intent.

definitions.text: Malfunctions, alongside malicious use and systemic risks, form the report's risk categories.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: A state in which humans cannot reliably monitor, constrain, correct or shut down AI systems.

definitions.text: Scenarios where models may resist human shutdown or control, now covered by frontier safety framework reviews.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Uncertainty from limited knowledge that could in principle be reduced by more evidence; dominant in this observatory.

definitions.text: Epistemic uncertainty stems from lack of knowledge and is reducible; aleatory uncertainty is inherent randomness.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.

items.short_definition: Irreducible randomness in outcomes even with complete knowledge of the process.

definitions.text: Aleatory uncertainty: inherent randomness that cannot be reduced by more data.

verification.note: Informational only; excluded from model computations until fetched and reviewed.
